warmup.q: Two threads each run count++ one million times on a shared int count = 0. What does count hold at the end, most of the time?
options: Less than 2,000,000, and a different number each run
warmup.why: Each count++ is a read, an add and a write. When both threads read the same old value, one of the two increments is lost. How many are lost depends on timing, so the result changes from run to run. Nothing throws: Java does not detect races for you.

sections.h: Two threads, one counter, the wrong answer
sections.html:
Here is the smallest broken program in this course. Two threads share one counter, and each adds one to it a million times.

Java
static volatile int count = 0;

Runnable work = () -> {
    for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) count++;
};
Thread a = new Thread(work), b = new Thread(work);
a.start(); b.start();
a.join(); b.join();
System.out.println(count);   // 2,000,000? Usually not.
Kotlin
@Volatile var count = 0

val work = { repeat(1_000_000) { count++ } }
val a = thread { work() }
val b = thread { work() }
a.join(); b.join()
println(count)               // 2,000,000? Usually not.

On my laptop five runs printed 1,851,852, then 1,633,408, then 1,920,984, then 1,599,468, then 2,000,000. Four wrong answers and one right one, from the same code.

This is a race condition: the result depends on how the threads happen to interleave. Nothing crashed. No exception, no warning, no log line. The program just did arithmetic wrong, and it did it differently each time.

Two details are worth knowing now.

The field is volatile (@Volatile in Kotlin) only to keep the demo honest. Without it the JIT compiler may keep count in a CPU register for the whole loop and write it back once at the end, which makes the lost updates disappear on some runs. That does not fix anything. It just hides the bug. volatile does not make count++ safe either; the memory model track shows exactly why.

The second detail matters more. Shrink the loop to 1,000 and every run prints the right answer. The first thread finishes before the second one even starts, so they never overlap. That is why races pass unit tests and fail under production traffic. A test that never makes threads collide proves nothing about thread safety.

try.title: Watch the counter lie
steps: Open RaceDemo.java (or its Kotlin twin, RaceDemo.kt) in the labs project. Before you run it, write down the number you expect.
Run it from labs/ with the command below. Note how many updates each run loses.
Run it again with -Pargs=1000 added. Predict first: will small loops lose updates?

code.title: RaceDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l03; /** Two threads each add 1,000,000 to a shared counter. Watch what comes out. */ public class RaceDemo { // volatile only stops the JIT from keeping count in a register, which would hide the race. // It does NOT make count++ safe. The memory model track explains why. static volatile int count = 0; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int perThread = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 1_000_000; for (int run = 1; run <= 5; run++) { count = 0; Runnable work = () -> { for (int i = 0; i < perThread; i++) count++; }; Thread a = new Thread(work), b = new Thread(work); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); System.out.printf("run %d: expected %,d, got %,d (lost %,d)%n", run, 2 * perThread, count, 2 * perThread - count); } } }

alt.title: RaceDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l03 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // @Volatile only stops the JIT from keeping count in a register, which would hide the race. // It does NOT make count++ safe. The memory model track explains why. @Volatile private var count = 0 /** Two threads each add 1,000,000 to a shared counter. Watch what comes out. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val perThread = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 1_000_000 for (run in 1..5) { count = 0 val work = { repeat(perThread) { count++ } } val a = thread { work() } val b = thread { work() } a.join(); b.join() println("run %d: expected %,d, got %,d (lost %,d)".format(run, 2 * perThread, count, 2 * perThread - count)) } }

try.expect: With a million per thread, most runs lose tens or hundreds of thousands of updates, and the number changes every run. With 1,000 per thread you almost always get exactly 2,000, because each thread finishes before the other gets going. Same bug, no symptom.

sections.h: count++ is three steps, not one
sections.html:
count++ looks like one operation. The JVM runs it as three. Here is the bytecode javac produces for it:

getstatic  count   // read the current value onto the stack
iconst_1           // push 1
iadd               // add them
putstatic  count   // write the result back

A thread can be paused between any two of those instructions. The operating system can move it off the CPU, or another core can run the same instructions at the same moment. So this can happen:

  1. T1 reads count: 41.
  2. T2 reads count: 41.
  3. T1 adds one and writes 42.
  4. T2 adds one and writes 42.

Two increments ran. The counter moved by one. This is a lost update, and the pattern behind it has a name: read-modify-write. You read a value, compute a new one from it, and write it back, while assuming nobody changed it in between.

Once you know the shape, you see it everywhere:

  • balance = balance - amount;
  • map.put(key, map.get(key) + 1);
  • total += invoice.amount();
  • list.add(x) on an ArrayList, which does size++ inside.

None of these is safe when two threads run it on shared data. The fix is always the same idea: the read and the write must happen as one step that no other thread can split. That property is called atomic.

The simulator below lets you play the scheduler. You pick which thread runs its next step. Try to make two increments end with count = 1. Then try to get 2. Notice that you need the threads to take turns on whole increments to get the right answer.

sim.title: Two threads run count++
sim.intro: You are the scheduler. Click a thread to run its next line. Can you end with count = 1?

goal.say: Lost update. Both threads read 0 before either wrote, so two increments produced 1.

try.title: See the three steps yourself
steps: Run the demo once (previous Try it) so Gradle compiles it.
From labs/, run the javap command below. It prints the bytecode of the class.
Find the lambda method (lambda$main$0) and the four lines that make up count++.
try.expect: Inside lambda$main$0 you'll see getstatic count, iconst_1, iadd, putstatic count. A thread can be paused between any two of them.

sections.h: Check-then-act: the race inside an if
sections.html:
The second shape of race hides in an if. You check a condition, then act on it, assuming the condition still holds.

Java
if (!owners.containsKey(seat)) {   // check
    owners.put(seat, passenger);   // act
    return true;
}
return false;
Kotlin
if (!owners.containsKey(seat)) {   // check
    owners[seat] = passenger       // act
    return true
}
return false

owners is a ConcurrentHashMap. Every single call on it is thread-safe. The code still sells the same seat twice, because the gap between containsKey and put belongs to nobody. Two buyers can both see the seat as free, and both go on to buy it. The second put silently replaces the first owner, and both callers got true.

This is the point most people miss: a thread-safe class does not make your code thread-safe. Each method is atomic. Two calls in a row are not.

The gap is often much wider than one line. Here is a version you may have written:

Java
if (!processed.contains(msg.idempotencyKey())) {
    ledger.charge(msg);                     // 80 ms call to the card issuer
    processed.add(msg.idempotencyKey());
}
Kotlin
if (msg.idempotencyKey !in processed) {
    ledger.charge(msg)                      // 80 ms call to the card issuer
    processed += msg.idempotencyKey
}

Kafka redelivers a message after a consumer rebalance, and two consumer threads pick up both copies. Both check the set during the same 80 ms. The customer pays twice.

Lazy initialization is the same shape: if (instance == null) instance = new Expensive(); can build two instances.

The fix is to let one operation do both the check and the act, so there is no gap:

Java
return owners.putIfAbsent(seat, passenger) == null;   // only one caller can see null
Kotlin
return owners.putIfAbsent(seat, passenger) == null    // same JDK call from Kotlin

putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, merge and Set.add (which returns false when the element was already there) all exist for this reason. Across machines, the same idea is a unique constraint in the database: insert the key first, and let the second insert fail.

try.title: Double-book a concert
steps: Run DoubleBookingDemo with the command below. Eight buyers race for 1,000 seats.
Change the check and the put into one call: if (owners.putIfAbsent(seat, me) == null) sold.incrementAndGet() in either version (keep the spin loop before it).

code.title: DoubleBookingDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l03; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Eight buyers race for the same 1,000 seats using check-then-act on a ConcurrentHashMap. */ public class DoubleBookingDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Map<Integer, String> owners = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); AtomicInteger sold = new AtomicInteger(); Thread[] buyers = new Thread[8]; for (int b = 0; b < buyers.length; b++) { String me = "buyer-" + b; buyers[b] = new Thread(() -> { for (int seat = 0; seat < 1_000; seat++) { if (!owners.containsKey(seat)) { // check for (int i = 0; i < 300; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); // a slow step owners.put(seat, me); // act sold.incrementAndGet(); } } }); } for (Thread t : buyers) t.start(); for (Thread t : buyers) t.join(); System.out.printf("seats: 1,000 tickets sold: %,d double-booked: %,d%n", sold.get(), sold.get() - 1_000); } }

alt.title: DoubleBookingDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l03 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** Eight buyers race for the same 1,000 seats using check-then-act on a ConcurrentHashMap. */ fun main() { val owners = ConcurrentHashMap<Int, String>() val sold = AtomicInteger() val buyers = (0 until 8).map { b -> thread(start = false) { for (seat in 0 until 1_000) { if (!owners.containsKey(seat)) { // check repeat(300) { Thread.onSpinWait() } // a slow step owners[seat] = "buyer-$b" // act sold.incrementAndGet() } } } } buyers.forEach { it.start() } buyers.forEach { it.join() } println("seats: 1,000 tickets sold: %,d double-booked: %,d".format(sold.get(), sold.get() - 1_000)) }

try.expect: The first run sells a few hundred tickets too many (one run here printed 1,413 tickets for 1,000 seats). After the change it sells exactly 1,000, every run, with the same slow step still inside the loop.

sections.h: What a fix has to do
sections.html:
Every fix for a race does two jobs. It makes the compound action atomic, so no other thread can run in the middle of it. And it makes the result visible, so the next thread to look sees the new value and not an old copy. Visibility gets its own track later. For now, know that the tools below give you both.

Here are your options, in the order I reach for them:

  1. Don't share. Give each thread its own counter and add them up at the end. Or keep the state inside one thread, such as one Kafka partition handled by one consumer. No sharing, no race.
  2. Use one atomic operation the library already has. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet(), LongAdder.increment(), ConcurrentHashMap.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum), putIfAbsent, Set.add. These are fast and hard to get wrong. Lesson 8 shows how they work.
  3. Lock the whole compound action. Mark the method synchronized so only one thread at a time can run it. This works for any code, including the slow 80 ms charge, but every caller now waits in line. Lesson 4 is about synchronized.

The lock must cover the read too. A synchronized setter with an unsynchronized getter is still broken, because the reader can see a stale value. And it must cover the whole action. Locking containsKey and put separately just gives you two atomic steps with the same gap between them.

For the counter, the cheapest correct fix is to put count++ inside a static synchronized void inc() method, or to swap the int for an AtomicInteger. Either way the demo prints 2,000,000 on every run.

try.title: Fix RaceDemo two ways
steps: In RaceDemo, add static synchronized void inc() { count++; } and call inc() in the loop. Run it.
Undo that. Change count to static final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger();, call count.incrementAndGet(), reset it with count.set(0) and print count.get(). Run it.
Which one felt slower? Add long t0 = System.nanoTime(); before the threads start and print the elapsed milliseconds after the joins to check.
try.expect: Both versions print exactly 2,000,000 on all five runs. On a typical laptop the atomic version is faster than the synchronized one when two threads fight over the counter, though both are much slower than the broken version. Correct code that does real synchronization costs something.

analogy: Picture two cashiers sharing one paper tally sheet. Each reads the total, adds their sale on a scrap of paper, and writes the new total over the old one. If both read 41 before either writes, both write 42 and one sale disappears from the books. The fix is to pass a single pen: whoever holds it does read, add and write before handing it over. The analogy breaks in one way: cashiers would notice the sheet changed under them. A CPU never notices. It writes 42 without complaint.
world: Look for the daily spend limit check in a payment service: if (spentToday + amount <= limit) { approve(); spentToday += amount; }. Two authorizations for the same card arrive 3 ms apart on two Quarkus worker threads. Both read spentToday before either adds to it, and the card goes over its limit. The same shape appears in Kafka consumers with concurrency above 1, in in-memory metrics counters, and in Temporal activities that check "already done?" before doing work. Activities can be retried, so make that check a single atomic step, ideally a database insert guarded by a unique key.
mistake: The most common mistake is trusting a thread-safe collection to make compound logic safe. ConcurrentHashMap, Collections.synchronizedMap and ConcurrentLinkedQueue make each method call atomic. They say nothing about two calls in a row. Code like if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) or map.put(k, map.get(k) + 1) is still a race. Reach for the single method that does the whole job: putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, merge or compute.

compare.title: The same race and fix in Java and Kotlin

java.title: HitCounter.java
java.html: public class HitCounter { private int count; // broken: count++ is read, add, write public void hitBroken() { count++; } // fixed: one thread at a time public synchronized void hit() { count++; } public synchronized int total() { return count; } }

kotlin.title: HitCounter.kt
kotlin.html: class HitCounter { private var count = 0 // broken: compiles to the same read, add, write fun hitBroken() { count++ } // fixed: Kotlin has no synchronized keyword; use the annotation @Synchronized fun hit() { count++ } @Synchronized fun total(): Int = count }

compare.note: Kotlin's count++ on a var property compiles to the same three bytecode steps, so it races in exactly the same way. Kotlin has no synchronized modifier. You write @Synchronized on a function, or call the standard library function synchronized(lock) { ... } with an explicit lock object. java.util.concurrent.atomic works the same from both languages.

worked.title: Find and fix the race in an idempotency check

steps.say: A payment handler skips messages it has already processed. It runs on four Kafka consumer threads. Read it and look for the shape before reading on.
steps.code: class PaymentHandler { private final Set<String> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); void handle(PaymentMessage m) { if (seen.contains(m.idempotencyKey())) return; // check ledger.charge(m); // 80 ms seen.add(m.idempotencyKey()); // act } }

alt.html: class PaymentHandler { private val seen: MutableSet<String> = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() fun handle(m: PaymentMessage) { if (m.idempotencyKey in seen) return // check ledger.charge(m) // 80 ms seen += m.idempotencyKey // act } }

steps.say: It is check-then-act. Two copies of the same message, handled by two threads within the same 80 ms, both pass the contains check. Both charge the card. The set being concurrent does not help, because the race is between the calls, not inside them.
Claim the key first, in one atomic call. Set.add returns false if the key was already there, so only one thread gets past this line. If the charge fails, release the claim so a retry can try again.
steps.code: void handle(PaymentMessage m) { if (!seen.add(m.idempotencyKey())) return; // check and act in one step try { ledger.charge(m); } catch (RuntimeException e) { seen.remove(m.idempotencyKey()); // let a retry have another go throw e; } }

alt.html: fun handle(m: PaymentMessage) { // 1. claim the key: add() returns false if it was already there if (!seen.add(m.idempotencyKey)) return try { ledger.charge(m) // 2. charge } catch (e: RuntimeException) { seen.remove(m.idempotencyKey) // 3. release on failure throw e } }

steps.say: That fixes the race inside one JVM. It does not survive a restart, and it does not cover two pods. In production the claim belongs in the database: insert the key into a table with a unique constraint before charging, and treat a duplicate-key error as "already processed". It is the same idea, one atomic step, moved to the place that all instances share.
steps.code: INSERT INTO processed_payment (idempotency_key, received_at) VALUES (?, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP); -- a second insert fails on the unique key

lab.title: Make threads collide, then fix two races
steps: Run the tests once. All five fail. Read the failure messages: the counter comes up short and seats are sold more than once.

Write Hammer.run. Create a CountDownLatch ready of size threads and a CountDownLatch go of size 1. Each thread calls ready.countDown(), waits on go.await(), then runs the task. The caller waits on ready, calls go.countDown(), then joins every thread.
Fix HitCounter so 8 threads x 200,000 hits always add up. Guard the read too.
Fix SeatMap.book without synchronized: replace the check and the put with one map call. Keep the call to priceTheSeat().
Run the tests again until all five pass. Run them three more times. Race fixes must pass every time.
hints: Why two latches in Hammer? ready tells the caller every thread exists and is parked. go releases them all at the same instant. Without ready, the first threads could finish before the last ones are created.
Inside a thread's lambda, go.await() throws InterruptedException. Catch it, restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(), and return.
putIfAbsent returns the previous value, or null if there was none. Only one caller can ever get null for a given key.
lab.done: All five tests in RaceConditionsTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the start-line harness from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page and the lab. In a blank file, write a method static void collide(int n, Runnable task) that starts n threads, releases them at the same moment, and returns when all are done. Then compare with the answer. Did you remember to join?

answer.html: static void collide(int n, Runnable task) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(n); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { ready.countDown(); try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; } task.run(); }); t.start(); threads.add(t); } ready.await(); // all parked at the start line go.countDown(); // starting gun for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); }

alt.html: fun collide(n: Int, task: () -> Unit) { val ready = CountDownLatch(n) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(n) { thread { ready.countDown() try { go.await() } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return@thread } task() } } ready.await() // all parked at the start line go.countDown() // starting gun threads.forEach { it.join() } }

recap: A race condition is a bug where the result depends on how threads interleave. It gives wrong answers silently.
Read-modify-write (count++, balance -= x, put(k, get(k) + 1)) loses updates when two threads read the same old value.
Check-then-act (if (!contains) put, if (x == null) x = new ...) breaks when another thread acts in the gap.
A thread-safe collection makes single calls atomic, never sequences of calls. Use putIfAbsent, merge, computeIfAbsent or Set.add.
Fixes, in order of preference: don't share, use one atomic library call, or lock the whole compound action including reads.
Races hide in small tests. Make threads collide on purpose, with a start latch, and run many iterations.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our seat map uses ConcurrentHashMap, so the booking code is thread-safe." Explain to them, in your own words, why that is wrong and what you would change.
explain.answer: ConcurrentHashMap makes each single call atomic, so containsKey and put are each safe on their own. The booking code runs them as two separate steps: check the seat, then take it. Another thread can take the seat between the two calls, so two buyers both see it free and both book it. The fix is to do the check and the act in one call, putIfAbsent(seat, buyer) == null, so only one caller can ever win. If many instances of the service share the seats, the same idea moves to a unique constraint in the database.

deeper.html:
Two terms sound alike and mean different things.

A data race is a precise term from the Java Language Specification, chapter 17. It happens when two threads access the same variable, at least one access is a write, and the two accesses are not ordered by a happens-before relationship. A program with a data race can see surprising values, because the compiler and CPU are allowed to reorder and cache unsynchronized accesses.

A race condition is a logic bug: the program is wrong under some interleavings. You can have one without the other. The fixed SeatMap has no data race, but if the code first called putIfAbsent and then, in a separate step, charged a card and rolled back on failure, other threads could still observe a seat that is sold and then unsold. That is a race condition built entirely from thread-safe calls. Going the other way, String.hashCode() caches its result in a plain field that several threads may write at once. That is a data race, but a benign one: every thread computes the same value, and int writes cannot tear.

long and double are the exception to that last point. JLS section 17.7 allows a write to a non-volatile long or double to happen as two separate 32-bit writes, so another thread could read half of an old value and half of a new one. 64-bit JVMs write them in one go in practice, but the spec does not promise it unless the field is volatile.

You'll meet happens-before properly in the memory model track. For now, the rule of thumb holds: every access to shared mutable state, reads included, goes through the same lock or the same atomic variable.
